intent: Make one shared language, structured around the domain model and spoken by domain experts and developers alike inside a bounded context, so code and conversation name the same thing.
problem: Developers use technical nouns and domain experts use business nouns for the same thing, so requirements are translated twice, the translation is lossy, and the defect that eventually appears was visible at the naming disagreement that nobody resolved.
context: Evans defines it as a language structured around the domain model and used by all team members within a bounded context to connect all the activities of the team with the software. It is scoped: the same term may legitimately carry different meanings in different contexts, and unifying it globally is the opposite of the idea. The language has to live somewhere — in code identifiers, in conversation, in documentation, in tests — and it is only ubiquitous when all of those agree and the model is exercised to hammer out disagreements as concepts evolve.
benefits: Requirements survive the trip from domain expert to code without a lossy translation.
Defects trace back to a definitional disagreement that can now be seen and settled.
Code reads as the domain, which makes it reviewable by people who are not programmers.
Onboarding a domain expert or a developer is far cheaper.
Ambiguity is surfaced early, when a word has two meanings — not at integration time.
tradeoffs: The language must be actively maintained; it decays silently when a term forks or is abbreviated.
It constrains naming: a domain term that is awkward as an identifier tempts divergence.
It is scoped per context, so the same real-world thing has different names in different parts of the system.
It requires domain experts and developers to actually work together, which is an organisational cost.
Code that mirrors a hastily-chosen vocabulary inherits its confusions.
quality_attributes_note: discoverability 10 by definition — the language is what a reader navigates by. security 5: the language is unrelated to threat modelling.

participants.responsibility: Uses the language with full meaning; the authority on what a term means.
participants.notes: Without them the language degrades into developer-invented jargon.

participants.responsibility: Uses the same words in code, tests and conversation.
participants.notes: With a ubiquitous language, the model is not just a design artifact — it becomes integral to everything developers and domain experts do together.

participants.responsibility: The structure the language is built around; the reason the words are precise.
participants.notes: The language exists to make a model usable; a glossary without a model is just a dictionary.

participants.responsibility: The scope in which each term has exactly one meaning.
participants.notes: Language is scoped; the same word may differ across contexts legitimately.

use_cases: Renaming `UserAccountRecord` to the term the business actually uses, so the class name matches the conversation.
Settling an argument about whether "closed" means cancelled or completed by writing it into the language.
Naming test cases after the domain scenarios rather than after the methods.
Rejecting a model that has no vocabulary a domain expert would recognise.
Splitting one word into two because it means two things in two contexts.
avoid_when: There is no domain expert available to supply or validate the vocabulary.
The project has no bounded context yet, so there is no scope in which the language can be defined.
A purely technical layer (transport, persistence plumbing) where domain vocabulary adds nothing.
A wire protocol or schema that must match an external standard — there the external names win and the language is translated.
pitfalls: A glossary document that drifts from the code; the code is the language, not the wiki.
Letting a developer invent a term for something the domain already names.
Trying to unify vocabulary across bounded contexts, which destroys both models.
Treating the ubiquitous language as documentation rather than as a design instrument.
Abbreviations that travel between the two communities and then mean one thing to each of them.

related_patterns_notes.bounded-context: The bounded context is the scope in which a ubiquitous language has exactly one meaning per term.
related_patterns_notes.readability-idiomatic-code: The generic reading principle is the same discipline applied to naming: the name carries the intent.
related_patterns_notes.published-language: A published language is the wire form of a ubiquitous language when it crosses a boundary to another team or system.
related_patterns_notes.intention-revealing-interface: An interface named after the domain concept rather than after its methods is the design-level expression of the same idea.

anti_patterns: An anemic entity layer named after database tables while the domain uses different words.
One "Client" class shared by three contexts that each mean something different by it.
A glossary maintained by one team and ignored by the rest.
Translating domain terms into more general programming terms (Manager, Handler, Worker) at the domain layer.
Naming by acronym, so the language is only decodable by the people who wrote it.
design_principles: A ubiquitous language is a language structured around the domain model and used by all team members within a bounded context to connect all the activities of the team with the software.
Modeling out loud; one team, one language.
Relentlessly exercise the ubiquitous language to hammer out a shared view of the model as concepts evolve in different people's heads.
Context determines the meaning of a word; statements about a model can only be understood in a context.
The greatest value of a domain model is that it provides a ubiquitous language that ties domain experts and technologists together.
best_practices: Use the domain term verbatim as the identifier; do not translate it into programming jargon.
Write test names as domain sentences so the language is exercised on every run.
Challenge any new term in a design review by asking what the business calls it.
Split a term into two names when it carries two meanings, rather than letting one name carry both.
Keep the language in the code and tests first; documentation follows the code, never leads it.
Review the vocabulary when a context is split, because vocabulary is what reveals the correct split.
